title: Ahmad ibn Hanbal

segments.voice: Yesterday, Egypt to Indonesia, and your line: by the monsoon. What crossed an ocean to reach your home, and who carried it? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-four.

An old man walks through Baghdad carrying an inkwell. Someone stops him. You've reached this rank, people call you an imam, and you still carry ink around like a student? His answer, in a saying reported of him: with the inkwell, to the grave. That's Ahmad ibn Hanbal. He was old, honored, and still a student of the reports, still copying them line by line. Today the Hanbali school begins, and it begins with a man who never stopped writing things down.
screen: `AN OLD MAN WITH AN INKWELL.` → `WITH THE INKWELL, TO THE GRAVE.` → `THE HANBALI SCHOOL BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Ahmad ibn Hanbal was a scholar of Baghdad, and above everything a scholar of hadith, the reports of what the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said and did. He traveled for them, his biographers say, to Kufa and Basra, to Mecca and Medina, and as far as Yemen, hearing reports from the people who carried them and writing them down. He also studied with al-Shafi'i, whose week this has been, and reports say each held the other in high regard. Here's what made his method his own. When a question came, he looked first to the Qur'an and the reports. Then to what the Companions had said. And reports say he would rather act on a weak hadith than on a jurist's analogy, as long as nothing stronger stood against it. Weak, here, doesn't mean made up. It means a chain of narrators with some doubt in it. For him, a report with some doubt was still closer to the Prophet than a clever argument. Some early writers even listed him among the scholars of hadith rather than among the jurists. His students saw it differently. They wrote down his answers to questions, one by one, about prayer, trade, marriage, manners, and out of those answers his school was built. So his law is a law of answers. Ask him something and the reply might be a report, passed on rather than argued. The imam of hadith is the one who kept the reports in front of the reasoning, and kept carrying the ink.
screen: `A SCHOLAR WHO TRAVELED FOR REPORTS.` · `A WEAK REPORT OVER A CLEVER ANALOGY.` · `A LAW OF ANSWERS.` · `AND KEEP CARRYING THE INK.`

segments.voice: The practice: memorize one hadith. Here's a short one, the report that opens Sahih al-Bukhari: actions are only by intentions. In Arabic, innamal a'malu bin-niyyat. Say it three times, slowly, in whichever language sits easier. Then close your eyes and say it once without help. Then let it work. Think of the next thing you'll do today, and ask what intention sits underneath it. If you pray, you can ask that your intentions be good ones. If not, just keep the line on your tongue. The bell holds the time.
Ahmad ibn Hanbal. The scholar of Baghdad who traveled for hadith, put reports before reasoning, and whose answers became the Hanbali school. Today's word.
Your line: the imam of hadith. Today, carry your hadith with you, and say it once before something that matters. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Hanbali scholars look first to the Qur'an and the hadith, then to the sayings of the Companions, and the school's rulings grew from Ahmad ibn Hanbal's recorded answers to questions.
